teaser: Three women at a summer dance. Or one woman, three times.
review_notes:
Dated 1899-1900 by the National Museum; '900' visible top right.
Dimensions 125 x 191 cm.
Munch's own description (first love, the flower that will not be picked, the woman in black) is paraphrased from his notes.
Tulla Larsen as model for the women in white and black; central woman linked to his first love Millie Thaulow: common readings, not certain.
Green-faced man identified by some writers as playwright Gunnar Heiberg: unproven.
Shooting incident with Tulla Larsen at Åsgårdstrand in 1902, Munch lost part of a finger of his left hand.
Frieze of Life shown as a full cycle in Berlin in 1902.
National Gallery acquired the painting in 1910: check.
Munch bought his house at Åsgårdstrand in 1898: check.

lesson.text: Which of these women is the oldest? The one in white on the left looks about twenty. The one in red, dancing in the middle, a little more. The one in black on the right has a drawn, tired face. Now compare the left and right faces: same features, same red-gold hair. Munch may be showing you a single life.

The setting is a real custom. On the shortest night of the year, around June 23, Norwegians light fires and dance outdoors by the water. Munch spent his summers in Åsgårdstrand, a fishing village on the Oslo fjord, where he bought a small yellow house in 1898. The curving shoreline behind the dancers is its beach.

He painted this big canvas, 125 by 191 centimeters (about 4 by 6 feet), in 1899 and 1900. Before reading any story into it, see how strictly it is arranged. A village dance is a jumble. This one is built like an altarpiece.
Munch organizes the party into a rigid, mirrored design.

lines.label: White
lines.text: A standing woman in white closes the left edge like a column. She faces inward, toward the couple.

lines.label: Black
lines.text: Her mirror image closes the right edge, same height, same stillness, also facing in. Only the color of the dress has changed.

lines.label: The couple
lines.text: Between them, the dancers are sealed inside one outline. His black suit and her red dress lock together like two pieces of a puzzle.

lines.label: The moon
lines.text: The moon and its reflection on the sea form an upright pillar. It stands exactly between the woman in white and the couple.

lesson.text: White, red, black: read from left to right, like a sentence. Munch explained the picture himself in his notes. The woman in white wants to pick the flower of love. The woman in red is in love's grip. The woman in black watches, shut out of the dance.

lesson.title: Three moments
lesson.text: The faces and the hands tell each stage.

spots.title: A hand, a flower
spots.text: She smiles, and her open hand drifts toward a spindly pink flower growing at her feet. She has not picked it yet. Her dress is scattered with gold blooms.

spots.title: Face to face
spots.text: The dancers' eyes are sunk in shadow, his nearly closed. His face is yellow-green. They do not smile. They look less like partners than sleepwalkers.

spots.title: The red hem
spots.text: Her dress pours over the grass and wraps around his feet. He could not step away if he tried.

spots.title: Clasped hands
spots.text: The woman in black holds her own hands tightly at her waist. No flower on this side of the picture. Her mouth is set, her eyes ringed with dark.

lesson.text: Did the couple feel like a tender moment to you? Most people sense the opposite: something heavy, almost a trance. For Munch love was never simple happiness. It was a force that takes people over, joins them, and then leaves them alone.

The pillar of moonlight is one of Munch's signatures. He painted the same shape, a disc on top of a bar of light, in picture after picture of the Åsgårdstrand shore. Many viewers have noticed it resembles a letter i, or something more bodily.

There was a real woman behind those two matching faces. In 1898 Munch began a relationship with Tulla Larsen, the red-haired daughter of a rich wine merchant. She wanted marriage. He, terrified of losing his freedom to paint, kept fleeing from city to city.

The dancing man is usually seen as Munch himself. In his notes he said he was dancing with his first love, a memory from years before. So the painter stands between a woman from his past and a woman who waits on both sides. The others on the grass are less dreamy.
One man in the background is not dancing gently. Find his face.

spots.title: The grinning man
spots.text: A bald, green face with red lips and bulging eyes pushes against a woman in white, who seems to bend away. Munch called the background couples a wild mob. This is desire at its crudest.

lesson.text: That leer changes the mood of the whole lawn. The other background couples spin with their faces left blank or turned away, pink ovals without features. Only the three women and the central pair have faces at all. They are the only individuals in a crowd of bodies.

The affair ended with a gunshot. During a quarrel with Tulla Larsen in his Åsgårdstrand house in 1902, a revolver went off and Munch lost part of a finger on his left hand. He never saw her again, and blamed her for the rest of his life.

The painting was made for a bigger plan. Munch thought of his main pictures as one long cycle he called the Frieze of Life, “a poem about life, love and death.” A frieze is a continuous band of images running along a wall. He showed the full cycle in Berlin in 1902, with this canvas as one of its largest pieces.

Munch hated to part with these pictures. He called his paintings his children, and when one from the Frieze was sold he often painted another version so the set would stay complete. He made a second Dance of Life in the 1920s.
The Dance of Life shrinks a lifetime into a single evening: hoping, having, losing. The colors do the telling. White for what has not happened yet, red for the present, black for what is over.

Norway's National Gallery acquired the painting in 1910, and it has stayed in Oslo since. Return to the first question. If the woman in white and the woman in black are the same person, which one is looking at the dancers, and which one is remembering them?

quiz.question: What do the three dress colors stand for, from left to right?
options: Hope before love, love itself, life after love
quiz.explanation: White, red and black mark three stages of one life.

quiz.question: What is the woman in white reaching toward?
quiz.explanation: Her open hand drifts toward a pink flower she has not yet picked.

quiz.question: What is the Frieze of Life?
options: A carved frame Munch made for this painting
A dance performed on midsummer night
Munch's cycle of paintings on life, love and death
quiz.explanation: He conceived his main pictures as one continuous series.

quiz.question: Where is the scene set?
options: On the shore at Åsgårdstrand, on a midsummer night
quiz.explanation: Munch spent his summers in this village on the Oslo fjord.

quiz.question: How do the central dancers look at each other?
options: With shadowed, nearly closed eyes and no smile
quiz.explanation: They seem locked in a trance more than enjoying a party.

quiz.question: What shape do the moon and its reflection make?
options: A circle of light around the dancers
An upright pillar on the water
A path leading to the right
quiz.explanation: Disc and reflection form a column, a motif Munch repeated often.

facts.text: The women in white and in black have clearly different faces and hair.
facts.explanation: They share the same features and red-gold hair, suggesting one woman at two moments.

facts.text: Munch's relationship with Tulla Larsen ended with a gunshot that injured his hand.
facts.explanation: A revolver went off during a quarrel in 1902 and he lost part of a finger.

facts.text: All the dancers in the background have carefully painted faces.
facts.explanation: Most are blank pink ovals; only one grinning man has features.
